analogy.p: Imagine people trying to get through a turnstile that only opens if they push hard enough (the activation energy) and facing the right way. A crowded station (higher concentration) means more people reach the turnstile each second; running (higher temperature) means more people push hard enough; a station with many turnstiles side by side is like a larger surface area; a catalyst is like a lower-friction turnstile that needs a lighter push. It breaks down because real particles are not choosing to queue and they collide randomly in three dimensions.

bullets: **Collision theory:** reaction requires (1) a collision, (2) with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy, and (3) the right orientation of the particles.
**Activation energy:** the minimum energy needed for a collision to be successful, shown on a reaction profile as the height from the reactants to the top of the energy hill.
**Rate of reaction** depends on the **frequency of successful collisions**, which is the number of successful collisions per second.
The **four factors** in the spec: temperature, concentration of solutions, pressure of gases and surface area of solids (a fifth, catalysts, has its own spec point).
You must **explain** each factor in terms of particles – 'collisions' alone is not enough; talk about **frequency** and **energy**.
You may be asked to compare reaction profiles with and without a catalyst, or exothermic with endothermic profiles.
Maths skills: surface area to volume ratio calculations, gradients of graphs, and reading values off energy diagrams.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA Chemistry 4.6.1.2 says that **chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy**. The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react is called the **activation energy**. You must be able to use this **collision theory** to explain how changing temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area (and, in the next topic, adding a catalyst) changes the rate of a reaction, and to draw and interpret **reaction profiles** that show activation energy. It is a core Paper 2 idea that links to energy changes, equilibrium and industrial processes, so it is examined in explanation questions worth 2 to 6 marks.

bullets: **A collision must occur:** particles cannot react at a distance. This is why reactants must be mixed or in contact.
**Sufficient energy:** the colliding particles must have a combined kinetic energy **equal to or greater than the activation energy**. This energy is needed to break the bonds in the reactants.
**Correct orientation:** the reactive parts of the particles must meet. In large molecules a collision with the wrong side facing can be unsuccessful even if the energy is high enough.
A collision that is not successful is sometimes called an **unsuccessful collision**; the particles rebound without reacting.
Only a **small fraction** of all collisions are successful at room temperature, which is why many reactions are slow.
**Rate of reaction ∝ frequency of successful collisions** – this is the sentence the mark scheme is built around.
Collision theory explains why the products form: bonds in the reactants are broken (energy needed), new bonds form (energy released).
core.h: The three conditions for a successful collision
core.p: A reaction between particles happens only when a collision is **successful**. Particles in solutions and gases are constantly moving randomly and bumping into each other, but most of these collisions do nothing because the particles just bounce apart. For a collision to lead to products it must meet the energy requirement and, for most reactions at GCSE level, the particles must be lined up correctly so that bonds can break and new bonds can form.

bullets: **Exothermic reaction:** the products are at a **lower** energy than the reactants; the overall energy change is negative (energy is **released** to the surroundings, so the temperature rises).
**Endothermic reaction:** the products are at a **higher** energy than the reactants; energy is **taken in** from the surroundings, so the temperature falls.
**Activation energy** is always drawn from the reactant level up to the top of the curve, never from the product level.
The **overall energy change** is drawn as an arrow between the reactant level and the product level.
The bigger the activation energy, the **smaller the proportion** of collisions that are successful, so the slower the reaction at a given temperature.
Exothermic reactions still need activation energy – that is why a match must be struck or a Bunsen lit before burning starts.
Labelling: axes 'progress of reaction' (x) and 'energy' (y); label reactants, products, activation energy and overall energy change.
A **catalyst** gives a profile with a lower peak (lower activation energy) but the same start and end levels.
core.p: A **reaction profile** is a graph of the energy of the particles against the progress of the reaction. Reactants start at one energy level, the profile rises to a peak (the **transition state**, the point of maximum energy), then falls to the energy level of the products. The height from the reactants to the peak is the **activation energy**; the difference in height between reactants and products is the **overall energy change** of the reaction.

bullets: **More frequent collisions** = more collisions per second because particles are closer together or have more exposed area.
**More energetic collisions** = particles hit with more energy, so a greater proportion exceed the activation energy.
At a higher temperature particles have more **kinetic energy**, so they move faster, and a greater proportion of collisions exceed activation energy.
At higher concentration, the **speed** and energy of each particle stays the same; only the number of particles in the volume increases.
**Successful collisions per second** is the combined effect of frequency and energy.
**Higher tier link:** a small rise in temperature can give a large rise in rate because the proportion of particles with at least the activation energy rises sharply.
In an answer say '**more frequent successful collisions**' or 'more **successful** collisions per second' to get the mark.
core.h: Frequency of collisions versus energy of collisions
core.p: Mark schemes separate two things that can change in a collision: **how often** particles collide (the frequency) and **how much energy** they have when they collide. Concentration, pressure and surface area increase only the **frequency** of collisions. Temperature increases **both** frequency and energy. Catalysts do neither; they provide a different pathway with a lower activation energy so a greater fraction of collisions are successful.

bullets: Mark scheme model: 'particles have more (kinetic) energy / move faster' + 'more frequent collisions' + 'more particles have energy greater than the activation energy' + 'more successful collisions'.
As a rough rule, for many reactions near room temperature the **rate approximately doubles for every 10 °C rise** in temperature – useful for estimates, but not a law.
The **activation energy itself does not change** with temperature; it is a property of the reaction.
Practical: heat the reactants in a water bath or on a hotplate and time the reaction; for the thiosulfate reaction the time for the cross to vanish decreases as temperature rises.
Food keeps longer in a fridge because lower temperatures slow the reactions that cause spoilage.
Industrial processes often use high temperatures, but cost and safety (and the effect on equilibrium yield) limit how high they go.
Exam trap: **frequency alone does not explain** why a small temperature rise has a big effect; mention energy too.
core.p: Raising the temperature increases the rate of reaction for **two reasons**. Firstly, the particles gain kinetic energy and **move faster**, so they **collide more frequently**. Secondly, and more importantly, a greater proportion of the collisions have energy equal to or greater than the **activation energy**, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful. Therefore the number of successful collisions per second increases and the rate goes up.

bullets: **x-axis:** kinetic energy of the particles; **y-axis:** number of particles with that energy.
The **activation energy** line stays in the **same place** when temperature changes because it is a property of the reaction.
**Higher temperature:** curve peak is **lower and further right**, with a **longer tail**, so the shaded area beyond Ea is larger.
The **area under both curves is equal** because there are the same number of particles.
A small temperature rise can produce a **large increase in the shaded fraction**, which is why rate rises quickly with temperature.
**Concentration and surface area** do not change the shape of the curve; they change **how often** particles meet.
A **catalyst** moves the Ea line **to the left**, so a larger fraction of particles is beyond it at the same temperature.
In an answer, say 'a greater **proportion** of collisions have energy ≥ Ea', not just 'more collisions are successful'.
core.h: Energy distribution of particles (why temperature matters so much)
core.p: In any sample of gas or solution the particles do not all have the same kinetic energy: most have a medium energy, a few have very little and a few have a lot. If you plot **number of particles against kinetic energy** you get a skewed hump. The activation energy is a **vertical line** on this graph, and only the particles in the shaded tail to the **right** of it can react when they collide. Raising the temperature moves the hump to the right and flattens it, but the **total number of particles (the area under the curve) stays the same**, so a **bigger fraction** of particles lies beyond the line. This is the Higher-tier idea behind the statement 'more of the particles have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy'.

bullets: Say 'more particles in the **same volume**' or 'particles are **closer together**'.
Do **not** say 'particles move faster' for concentration or pressure – that is temperature.
For gases, doubling the pressure doubles the number of particles in a given volume (at constant temperature) and so roughly doubles the collision frequency.
Only reactants that are **gases** are affected by pressure; changing pressure has no useful effect on reactions of only solids and liquids.
As a reaction proceeds, the reactant concentration falls, so the rate **decreases** and the graph flattens.
Evidence from the practical: rate (1/t) is directly proportional to concentration for the thiosulfate reaction.
Industrial gas reactions (such as the Haber process at about 200 atmospheres) use high pressure to increase rate (and yield) but the equipment is expensive.
core.p: Increasing the **concentration** of a reactant in solution means there are **more particles of that reactant in the same volume**. The particles are closer together, so collisions are **more frequent**, so the frequency of successful collisions increases and the rate rises. For **gases**, increasing the **pressure** pushes the same number of gas particles into a smaller volume, which has the same effect as increasing concentration. In both cases the energy of the particles is unchanged.

bullets: **Surface area to volume ratio = surface area ÷ volume**, in units such as cm⁻¹ (cm2/cm3).
**Cube worked idea:** a 1 cm cube has surface area 6 cm2 and volume 1 cm3, ratio **6:1**; a 2 cm cube has surface area 24 cm2 and volume 8 cm3, ratio **3:1**. The smaller cube has the larger ratio.
Cutting a 2 cm cube into eight 1 cm cubes keeps the volume 8 cm3 but increases the total surface area to 8 × 6 = 48 cm2, so the ratio doubles to **6:1**.
**Powdered** marble reacts much faster than marble chips with acid because the powder has a larger surface area to volume ratio.
**Dust explosions** (flour, coal, sugar) happen because very fine powder has huge surface area, burns very fast, and is spread through the air.
Nanoparticles have a very large surface area to volume ratio, so even small amounts can be very reactive or effective as catalysts.
**Practical:** use the same mass of marble chips of different sizes and compare the rate of CO2 production.
Say 'larger surface area to volume ratio, so **more particles exposed** and **more frequent collisions**'.
core.h: Effect of surface area of solids and the surface area to volume ratio
core.p: For reactions involving a **solid** and a liquid or gas, the reaction can only happen where the particles in the solid are exposed on the **surface**. Breaking a solid into smaller pieces (or a powder) creates more exposed surface for the same total mass, so the **surface area to volume ratio** increases. More solid particles are therefore exposed to the other reactant, collisions are **more frequent** and the rate is higher. Particles in the inside of a lump cannot collide with the other reactant until the outside has reacted away.

bullets: **Count particles** in equal volumes in a diagram to compare concentrations (for example 6 versus 14).
**Surface area of a cube** = 6 × side²; **volume** = side³; SA:V = 6 ÷ side, so halving the side **doubles** the ratio.
Cutting a solid does **not change its volume or mass**, only the surface exposed to the other reactant.
A **gradient** steeper at the start means a higher initial rate; the final volume depends on the **limiting reactant**.
**Rate** can be found as change in quantity ÷ time, or the gradient of a tangent (Higher tier).
Collision theory explains **why** a factor changes the rate; it does not change the **amount of product** formed.
Link to the **required practical** on rates: marble chips + acid (gas volume or mass loss) and sodium thiosulfate + acid (time for a cross to disappear).
core.h: Using particle diagrams and numbers to explain each factor
core.p: Examiners often show a **particle diagram** or a **table of data** and ask you to explain a change in rate. For **concentration** you compare how many particles of the reactant are in the **same volume**; for a **gas** the pressure is higher when the same gas is squeezed into a smaller volume. For a **solid** you compare the **surface area to volume ratio**: a 2 cm cube has surface area 6 × 2² = 24 cm² and volume 2³ = 8 cm³, so SA:V = 3 : 1, but eight 1 cm cubes have a total surface area of 8 × 6 = 48 cm² with the same total volume of 8 cm³, so SA:V = 6 : 1. In every case finish the chain: more particles exposed or closer together → **more frequent collisions** → more **successful collisions per second** → higher rate.

bullets: A catalyst does **not** change the **energy of the reactants and products** or the overall energy change.
On a reaction profile the catalysed peak is **lower**; start and end levels are the same.
A catalyst is **not used up**, so it can be reused; but it may become poisoned or lose surface area over time.
A catalyst does not increase the **yield** in a reversible reaction at equilibrium; it reaches equilibrium faster.
Different reactions need different catalysts; **enzymes** are biological catalysts.
Catalysts reduce the temperature needed, saving energy and cost in industry.
Wording: 'provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy' – use these words exactly.
core.p: A **catalyst** is a substance that **speeds up a reaction without being used up** in the reaction. It works by providing an **alternative reaction pathway** with a **lower activation energy**. With a lower activation energy, a greater proportion of collisions are successful at the same temperature, so the number of successful collisions per second increases. The detail, including enzymes, is covered in the catalyst spec point, but you should apply it to collision theory here.

bullets: **Gradient = rate:** steep = fast, shallow = slow, flat = no change (reaction finished).
If reactants are in excess, the **final amount of product** depends only on the limiting reactant, not the concentration of the excess one.
Two experiments that use the same mass of limiting reactant end at the **same final volume** but at different times.
A reaction that gets warmer (exothermic) may speed up slightly at first then slow down as reactants deplete.
For a mass-loss graph, the curve is the same shape, with the final mass lower than the initial.
If you compare two curves, say which has the steeper gradient at the start and link to the rate factor changed.
Higher tier: the rate at a particular time is the gradient of the tangent at that time.
core.h: Why the rate changes as a reaction proceeds
core.p: During most reactions the rate is highest at the start and then **falls**. This happens because reactants are used up, so their concentration falls, so collisions become **less frequent** and fewer successful collisions occur per second. The reaction stops when one of the reactants (the **limiting reactant**) is completely used up. In a graph of product against time the line is steepest at the start (maximum gradient) and becomes **horizontal** at the end.

bullets: **Steeper line, same final volume:** a faster rate with the same amount of reactant: higher temperature, higher concentration, powder instead of lumps, or a catalyst.
**Higher final volume:** a greater amount of the limiting reactant was used.
**Rate calculation:** mean rate = change in quantity ÷ time; with tangents (HT) rate at a given moment.
**Comparing two experiments:** quote numbers – 'at 20 s the volume is 30 cm3 for A and 18 cm3 for B, so A is faster'.
Link the cause to particles in a three-step chain: change → effect on particles → effect on collisions → effect on rate.
Use the term 'successful collisions' when you mention energy and 'frequent' when you mention number of collisions.
Be careful with questions about temperature: also mention the proportion of particles with **energy greater than the activation energy**.
core.h: Explaining graphs and data in terms of collision theory
core.p: Exam questions give you data or a graph and ask you to **identify which factor has changed** and **explain the result**. Use the evidence: the curve with the steeper initial gradient has the faster rate, so a higher temperature, concentration or surface area (or a catalyst). If the plateau is at the same level, the amount of limiting reactant was the same. If the plateau is **higher**, more reactant was used.

bullets: In an **exothermic** reaction more energy is released making bonds in products than is needed to break bonds in reactants.
In an **endothermic** reaction more energy is needed to break bonds than is released making new bonds.
In a reversible reaction, the forward and reverse reactions have different activation energies; one is exothermic and the other endothermic by the same amount.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy for **both** the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium position is unchanged.
Higher temperature increases the rate of **both** directions in a reversible reaction but shifts the equilibrium position towards the endothermic direction.
In industry, rate and yield conditions are balanced (e.g. Haber process: 450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst).
Energy profiles for catalysed and uncatalysed reactions show why catalysts save energy.
core.h: Link to bond energies, energy changes and equilibrium
core.p: The activation energy corresponds to the energy needed to **start breaking bonds** in the reactants. Overall energy change is the balance between energy needed to break old bonds and energy released when new bonds form. This links collision theory to **exothermic and endothermic reactions** (4.5) and to **dynamic equilibrium** (4.6.2), where the forward and reverse reactions each have their own activation energy.

bullets: **Fridge and freezer:** lower temperature, fewer energetic collisions, so food spoils slowly.
**Pressure cooker:** higher pressure raises the boiling point of water so food cooks at a higher temperature and faster.
**Dust explosions:** fine powders have a large surface area to volume ratio, so burn extremely quickly.
**Antacid tablets:** crushed tablets neutralise stomach acid faster than whole ones.
**Lighting a fire:** logs burn slowly, kindling and paper burn fast – smaller pieces have more surface area; the match supplies the activation energy.
**Catalytic converters:** platinum or rhodium catalysts speed up reactions removing CO and NOx from exhaust gases.
**Powdered versus lump sugar:** powdered sugar dissolves faster because of greater surface area.
**Industry:** the Haber process uses an iron catalyst, 450 °C and 200 atm to give an economic rate.
core.p: Collision theory explains many everyday and industrial observations. In each case identify the factor changed, then explain it in terms of particles. Good answers use the language of **frequency of collisions** and **successful collisions**.

bullets: **Surface area of a cube** = 6 × (side)2; **volume** = (side)3; SA:V = 6 ÷ side.
Check: side 1 cm → 6 cm⁻¹; side 2 cm → 3 cm⁻¹; side 0.5 cm → 12 cm⁻¹.
**Gradient** = Δy ÷ Δx: use a large triangle, state units (cm3/s).
**Rate ratio:** if the rate doubles, the time taken for a fixed amount of reaction halves.
**Activation energy from a profile:** energy at peak − energy of reactants (e.g. 350 − 200 = 150 kJ/mol).
**Overall energy change** = energy of products − energy of reactants (e.g. 120 − 200 = −80 kJ/mol, exothermic).
Proportion of particles above the activation energy rises sharply with temperature; at GCSE you describe this in words only.
core.h: Maths skills and Higher tier extensions
core.p: The collision theory topic uses several maths skills: **surface area and volume calculations**, ratios, **gradients of graphs**, proportionality and interpreting energy-profile diagrams. In calculations, always show units and, for ratios, simplify. Higher tier students may be asked to relate the rate to the **gradient of a tangent** or to evaluate why a small change in temperature has a large effect.

bullets: **Temperature (3–4 marks):** particles have more kinetic energy/move faster; collide more frequently; more particles have energy ≥ activation energy; more successful collisions per second.
**Concentration/pressure (2–3 marks):** more particles in the same volume; collisions more frequent; more successful collisions per second.
**Surface area (2–3 marks):** more particles exposed/larger SA:V; more frequent collisions; higher rate.
**Catalyst (2 marks):** provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy; more particles have enough energy; more successful collisions.
**Reaction profile:** labelled axes, reactants and products at the correct levels, peak, activation energy arrow from the reactants, overall energy change arrow.
**Never** write 'more collisions' – write '**more frequent collisions**'; do not say 'the activation energy decreases' for temperature or concentration.
Use the numbers in the question; quote values when comparing graphs.
If asked to compare, mention both: 'the rate is higher because …, whereas the final volume is the same because …'.
core.p: Collision theory questions reward **precision of language** and a clear chain of reasoning. The 'explain' command word means give reasons, linking cause to effect with 'because' and 'so'. Use all the marking points for each factor, because examiners usually allocate one mark per idea.

exam: **Command words:** 'explain' needs reasons ('because… so…'); 'describe' needs what happens; 'suggest' applies knowledge to an unfamiliar context.
**1 mark:** define activation energy; state a factor; name a catalyst; label a profile.
**2 marks:** 'more particles in the same volume' + 'more frequent collisions' for concentration.
**3 marks:** temperature – faster, more frequent collisions; more particles with energy ≥ activation energy; more successful collisions.
**4 marks:** two linked ideas for each of two factors or a comparison of graphs with evidence.
**6 marks:** a coherent explanation covering several factors, linking each to frequency and energy, using data from the question.

**Reaction profile questions:** draw reactants at one level, products lower (exo) or higher (endo), a smooth peak, an arrow for activation energy from reactants, and a catalysed curve with a lower peak.
**Graph tips:** steeper gradient = faster; compare initial gradients; same final volume = same amount of limiting reactant.
**Calculation tips:** SA:V = surface area ÷ volume, show working, give units; Ea = peak − reactants.
**Avoid:** 'more collisions' without 'frequent', 'temperature lowers the activation energy', and 'the catalyst is used up'.
**Energy distribution graph (3 marks):** higher temperature curve peak lower and to the right; Ea line unchanged; larger shaded area beyond Ea.

mistakes.r: Activation energy is unchanged by temperature; more particles have energy equal to or greater than it.
mistakes.w: Increasing the temperature makes the activation energy lower.

mistakes.r: More frequent collisions and a higher frequency of successful collisions.
mistakes.w: More collisions, so the rate is faster.

mistakes.r: Speed depends on temperature; higher concentration means more particles in the same volume.
mistakes.w: A higher concentration makes the particles move faster.

mistakes.r: It is the minimum energy needed for a collision to be successful, measured from reactants to the peak.
mistakes.w: Activation energy is the energy released by the reaction.

mistakes.r: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy; it does not supply energy.
mistakes.w: A catalyst provides energy for the reaction.

mistakes.r: All reactions need activation energy; exothermic ones just release more energy than they absorb overall.
mistakes.w: Exothermic reactions do not need activation energy.

mistakes.r: The mass is the same; the total surface area (and SA:V ratio) increases because it is broken into smaller pieces.
mistakes.w: Surface area increases because the solid is smaller in total.

mistakes.r: The reaction stops because one reactant has been used up.
mistakes.w: The reaction stops because the particles run out of energy.

mistakes.r: Draw it from the reactants level to the peak.
mistakes.w: Draw the activation energy arrow from the products to the peak.

mistakes.r: The activation energy stays the same; a greater proportion of particles has energy ≥ Ea.
mistakes.w: Raising the temperature lowers the activation energy.

summary: AQA 4.6.1.2: reactions happen only when particles collide with at least the activation energy (and the right orientation). You must use collision theory to explain how temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area change the frequency and success of collisions, and draw and read reaction profiles. It underpins every rate and industrial-conditions question on Paper 2.

terms.d: Chemical reactions can only occur when reacting particles collide with each other with sufficient energy.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react.
A collision in which the particles have at least the activation energy (and the right orientation), so that a reaction occurs.
The number of collisions per second between reacting particles.
How fast reactants are used up or products formed; depends on the frequency of successful collisions.
The amount of a substance in a given volume of solution; more particles per unit volume means higher concentration.
Increasing the pressure of a gas squeezes the particles into a smaller volume, increasing their concentration.
The surface area of an object divided by its volume; increases as a solid is broken into smaller pieces.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up, by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
A diagram showing the relative energies of reactants and products and the activation energy of a reaction.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases; products have less energy than reactants.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases; products have more energy than reactants.
The energy of a particle due to its movement; increases with temperature.
The reactant that is completely used up first and so determines the amount of product formed.
The difference in energy between the products and the reactants of a reaction.
A straight line touching a curve at one point, whose gradient gives the rate at that time (Higher tier).
The way round particles are when they collide; the reactive parts must meet for a successful collision.
Graph showing how many particles have each kinetic energy; only the tail above Ea can react.
The point of maximum energy on a reaction profile (the peak) as bonds break and form.

worked.q: [3 marks] A cube of calcium carbonate has sides of 2 cm. (a) Calculate its surface area to volume ratio. (b) It is cut into eight cubes of side 1 cm. Calculate the new ratio and state the effect on the rate of reaction with acid.
steps: (a) Surface area = 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cm2; volume = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm3; ratio = 24 ÷ 8 = 3.
(b) Each small cube: surface area 6 cm2, volume 1 cm3, ratio 6; total area 8 × 6 = 48 cm2, volume 8 cm3, ratio 48 ÷ 8 = 6.
The ratio doubles, so more particles are exposed to the acid and collisions are more frequent.

worked.ans: At a higher temperature the particles have more energy and move faster, so collisions are more frequent. More of the particles have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful. Therefore the frequency of successful collisions increases and the rate of reaction increases.
worked.q: [4 marks] Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction.
steps: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster.
A greater proportion of collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.
So the number of successful collisions per second increases.

worked.q: [4 marks] A reaction profile shows reactants at 200 kJ/mol, a peak at 350 kJ/mol and products at 120 kJ/mol. A catalyst lowers the peak to 280 kJ/mol. (a) Calculate the activation energy without a catalyst. (b) Calculate the overall energy change and state whether it is exothermic or endothermic. (c) Calculate the activation energy with the catalyst.
steps: (b) Overall energy change = 120 − 200 = −80 kJ/mol; products have less energy so energy is released: exothermic.
(c) Ea with catalyst = 280 − 200 = 80 kJ/mol; the overall energy change is still −80 kJ/mol.
